What runtime security would you add?
How do you protect the mesh control plane?

questions.q: Define the operating model for the mesh: what the platform team owns, what application teams own, and how changes and incidents flow.
questions.a:
### Ownership
| Platform team | Application teams |
|---|---|
| control plane, ztunnel/waypoints or sidecar injection, upgrades | their namespace's routes (HTTPRoute/VirtualService) within guardrails |
| PKI integration, root and intermediate lifecycle | inbound AuthorizationPolicies for their services |
| mesh-wide defaults (STRICT, export scoping, telemetry) | timeouts and retries for their dependencies within caps |
| admission guardrails, linting, golden-path templates | canary configuration via rollout tooling |
| egress gateways and ServiceEntry approval | requesting egress for new external hosts |
| mesh SLOs, dashboards, runbooks, on-call for mesh faults | on-call for their services |

### Change flow
Application mesh config lives with the app (Helm chart or kustomize), validated by the same CI guardrails; platform changes go through progressive rollout (revisions, canary namespaces). Access requests between teams are pull requests against the **target** team's inbound policy.

### Incident flow
Runbooks start with "is it the mesh?" (response flags, proxy sync status, platform dashboards). Platform on-call joins any incident where mesh signals are abnormal; app teams own resolution otherwise.

### Measures
Platform SLOs (control-plane availability, config propagation time, certificate issuance success), mesh-caused incidents per quarter, and developer satisfaction.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Platform SLOs for the mesh (published)
slos:
  - name: control-plane-availability
    sli: istiod and ztunnel ready replicas meet minimum
    objective: 99.95%
  - name: config-propagation
    sli: p99 time from config apply to all relevant proxies SYNCED
    objective: "< 30s for 99% of changes"
  - name: certificate-issuance
    sli: successful CSR signing ratio
    objective: 99.99%
  - name: data-plane-overhead
    sli: added p99 latency per hop (ambient L4)
    objective: "< 1ms"
escalation:
  mesh_signals: [proxy_status_stale, xds_rejects, cert_issuance_errors, ztunnel_restarts]
  page: platform-mesh-oncall
~~~
pts: Platform owns runtime, PKI, defaults and guardrails.
Teams own their routes and inbound policies within caps.
Access requests are PRs to the target's policy.
Runbooks start with mesh health signals.
Publish platform SLOs.
questions.ex: Without clear ownership, every 503 became a "mesh problem" and the platform team was paged 60 times a month. Runbooks keyed on response flags and proxy health cut platform pages to under 10, with app teams resolving their own routing issues.

How do you handle cross-team policy disputes?
What is a reasonable platform team size?
pit: Platform as the help desk for all networking.
Teams editing other teams' inbound policies.

questions.q: Build the cost model for a mesh at 3,000 pods. What are the direct and indirect costs, and which choices change them most?
questions.a:
### Direct costs
| Item | Driver |
|---|---|
| Sidecar CPU and memory requests | per pod (for example 0.1 vCPU and 128 MB request each: 300 vCPU and 384 GB for 3,000 pods) |
| ztunnel and waypoints (ambient) | per node and per L7 namespace |
| Control plane | replicas sized by config size and push rate |
| Telemetry | metrics series (pairs x labels), traces, access logs: often larger than compute |
| Gateways | ingress, egress, east-west replicas |
| Cross-zone traffic | locality settings |

### Indirect costs
Platform team salaries, upgrade effort, incident time, developer learning, vendor support.

### Biggest levers
1. **Ambient instead of sidecars**: removes per-pod overhead.
2. **Right-size proxy requests** from measured usage (sidecar defaults are often oversized or undersized).
3. **Sidecar or config scoping** to cut proxy memory.
4. **Telemetry tuning**: drop unused labels, sample traces, error-only access logs.
5. **Locality-aware routing** to reduce cross-zone transfer.

### Benefits to price
Avoided per-team implementation of TLS, retries and telemetry; audit evidence effort; incident reduction from consistent policies.
pts: Direct: proxies, control plane, telemetry, gateways, transfer.
Indirect: platform team, upgrades, incidents, learning.
Ambient removes per-pod overhead.
Telemetry tuning often saves the most.
Price avoided duplication and audit effort.
questions.ex: A cost review found the mesh's Prometheus series (pair x response code x flags) cost more than all sidecars combined. Dropping two labels and sampling traces at 5% cut mesh telemetry cost by 65%; moving to ambient cut proxy compute by 70%.
fu: How do you right-size sidecar requests?
How do you attribute mesh cost to teams?
What does a managed add-on cost?
pit: Default proxy requests for all pods.
No benefit side in the model.

questions.q: Design mesh topology for an active-active two-region platform where some services are stateless and others own regional data. How do you prevent the mesh from creating cross-region surprises?
questions.a:
### Topology
Multi-primary single mesh per jurisdiction (for example EU West and EU North), separate networks with east-west gateways, shared root CA (or federated intermediates).

### Service classes
| Class | Mesh behaviour |
|---|---|
| Stateless (quotes, reference data) | locality LB with cross-region failover |
| Regional-data owners (ledger per region) | **no cross-region routing**: restrict endpoints to local cluster ({{trafficDistribution}} or locality settings with no failover), failover is a data-layer decision |
| Global singletons (scheduler) | explicit home region, failover by runbook |

### Preventing surprises
- Default locality preference so calls stay local; cross-region failover only for opted-in services.
- Timeouts sized for local latency; a failover to a remote region should trip circuit breakers rather than silently slow everything.
- Dashboards showing **cross-region request rate** per service pair: should be near zero normally.
- Config changes rolled out per region.
- Async data replication handled by data platforms (database replication, Kafka mirroring), not the mesh.

### Failure drills
Kill a region's ingress, a service's local endpoints, and the east-west gateway; verify expected behaviour for each class.

Cross-region failover only for opted-in stateless services.

questions.q: Postmortem: the mesh's intermediate CA expired on a Saturday and new pods couldn't get certificates, leading to a cascading outage. Run the review and the systemic fixes.
questions.a:
### Timeline pattern
Intermediate expires; existing workload certs (24 h) keep working until rotation; rotations fail; certs expire over the following hours; autoscaled and restarted pods can't join; outbound mTLS starts failing; health checks fail; restarts amplify the problem.

### Contributing factors
- Expiry not monitored (or alert routed to an unowned channel).
- Rotation was manual and undocumented; the person who did it last left.
- No staging rehearsal of rotation.
- Workload certificate lifetime meant a delay before symptoms, obscuring the cause.

### Fixes
| Area | Fix |
|---|---|
| Detection | expiry alerts at 90, 45, 14, 7 days, routed to platform on-call; certificate issuance failure alerts |
| Automation | intermediate issuance and rotation automated (cert-manager, Vault) with dual-chain trust bundles |
| Rehearsal | quarterly rotation in staging; annual in production during business hours |
| Runbook | emergency procedure to issue a new intermediate and push trust bundle, practised |
| Design | longer intermediate lifetime with automated renewal well before expiry; monitoring of workload cert age distribution |
| Ownership | named owner for PKI lifecycle; on-call coverage |

### Culture
Blameless: the failure was a missing system, not a person.

questions.q: Migrate 60 namespaces from Istio sidecar mode to ambient without losing security guarantees. Plan the migration.
questions.a:
### Preconditions
Istio version with GA ambient, CNI compatibility verified, node agents (ztunnel) capacity planned, observability for ambient metrics in place.

### Policy translation (the critical part)
- L4-only AuthorizationPolicies (principals, namespaces, ports) work at ztunnel.
- L7 policies (paths, methods, JWT) must move to **waypoints** with {{targetRefs}}; inventory every L7 policy and VirtualService first.
- VirtualService features (retries, canaries) also require waypoints; prefer Gateway API HTTPRoutes for new config.
- RequestAuthentication requires a waypoint for enforcement.

### Per-namespace steps
1. Deploy a waypoint if the namespace needs L7.
2. Retarget L7 policies and routes to the waypoint; verify with {{istioctl analyze}}.
3. Label namespace for ambient, remove injection label, restart pods to remove sidecars.
4. Verify: mTLS (ztunnel metrics), policy denials still occur for forbidden calls (automated negative tests), latency and error rates.
5. Keep rollback: relabel for sidecar injection and restart.

### Order
Low-risk namespaces with L4-only needs first; L7-heavy namespaces later; payments last with change windows.
questions.code:
~~~bash
ns=statements
# 1-2. Waypoint and retargeted L7 policies (applied from Git)
istioctl waypoint apply -n $ns --enroll-namespace
kubectl apply -n $ns -f policies/l7-targetref/
istioctl analyze -n $ns                                   # warns on L7 policies not bound to a waypoint

# 3. Switch data plane
kubectl label namespace $ns istio-injection- istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n $ns                     # pods come back without sidecars

# 4. Verify negative test: forbidden caller must be denied
kubectl run deny-probe -n reporting --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://statements-api.$ns:8080/admin   # expect 403
~~~
pts: Inventory L7 policies and routes before migrating.
L7 requires waypoints and targetRefs.
Per namespace: waypoint, retarget, relabel, restart, verify.
Automated negative tests prove enforcement.
L4-only namespaces first, payments last.
questions.ex: A migration pilot showed a JWT-requiring policy was silently unenforced after switching to ambient because no waypoint existed. The plan was changed so CI blocks any namespace switch while istioctl analyze reports unbound L7 policies.

questions.q: Design the zero-trust service-to-service architecture for a regulated bank. Where does the mesh fit among identity, policy, data and monitoring controls?
questions.a:
### Pillars
1. **Workload identity**: SPIFFE identities via mesh (Kubernetes), certificates for VMs, cloud workload identity for PaaS.
2. **Strong authentication on every hop**: mTLS STRICT everywhere; no plaintext exceptions without expiry.
3. **Authorisation**: default deny in mesh (service level), plus user context (JWT, token exchange) and application object-level checks, optionally a central policy engine (OPA, Cedar) for consistent rules.
4. **Network segmentation**: NetworkPolicies, separate clusters or meshes for PCI and critical systems, egress allow-lists.
5. **Data protection**: encryption at rest, tokenisation, field-level encryption for PII.
6. **Continuous verification and monitoring**: telemetry on denials and anomalies, runtime security (eBPF detection), regular control tests.
7. **Supply chain**: signed images, admission control, SBOMs.

### Mesh's role
Provides 1 and 2 uniformly for Kubernetes, the service-level part of 3, telemetry for 6, and evidence. It is one enforcement point among several.

### Governance
Control objectives mapped to regulations (DORA, PCI DSS, local regulator guidelines), evidence automated, exceptions risk-accepted by named owners.

questions.q: The mesh is causing more problems than it solves for a business unit. How would you decide to remove it, and how do you exit safely?
questions.a:
### Decide with evidence
- Which goals was the mesh meant to achieve (mTLS evidence, authz, telemetry)? Are they met? Could they be met otherwise?
- Incidents caused by the mesh vs prevented; overhead; team time spent.
- Is the problem the mesh, or the mode (sidecar overhead fixable by ambient), or ownership (no platform team)?

### If exiting
1. **Replace each capability** before removal:
   - mTLS: app-level TLS with cert-manager certificates, or CNI encryption.
   - Service authz: OAuth client credentials and audience checks; NetworkPolicies.
   - Resilience: resilience handlers in code (shared defaults package).
   - Telemetry: OpenTelemetry in services.
   - Traffic shifting: Argo Rollouts with ingress or Gateway API.
2. Run both in parallel per namespace (mesh in PERMISSIVE while app TLS is enabled), verify.
3. Remove injection or ambient label; restart; verify negative tests still fail as expected.
4. Remove mesh CRDs and control plane after all namespaces exit.
5. Update audit evidence and control mappings.

### Reversibility lesson
Keep mesh-specific config in a small number of well-understood resources; prefer portable APIs (Gateway API) so either direction stays possible.
pts: Decide with evidence: goals, incidents, overhead, alternatives.
Check whether the mode or ownership is the real problem.
Replace every capability before removal.
Parallel run and negative tests per namespace.
Prefer portable APIs to keep reversibility.

questions.q: Developers say the mesh makes local development and debugging harder. How do you reduce cognitive load while keeping the mesh's guarantees?
questions.a:
### Pain points
- Local environment doesn't behave like the mesh (no mTLS, no policies), so issues appear only in clusters.
- Opaque 503s and RBAC 403s.
- YAML-heavy configuration in unfamiliar CRDs.
- Debugging requires istioctl knowledge.

### Remedies
| Remedy | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Golden-path templates**: Helm or kustomize charts that generate correct mesh config from a few values (dependencies, routes, canary) | teams declare intent, not Envoy details |
| **Error transparency**: response flags surfaced in logs, a "why was I denied" tool (authz check), dashboards per service | faster self-service debugging |
| **Dev clusters or ephemeral environments with the mesh** (or mirrord/Telepresence to connect local processes into the cluster) | realistic behaviour early |
| **Policy linting in CI with clear messages** | failures before deploy |
| **Docs as runbooks**: "my call returns 503 NR" pages | common issues solved in minutes |
| **Ambient mode** | fewer lifecycle surprises, no sidecar containers |

### Principle
Developers shouldn't need to know Envoy. The platform's API to them is "my service calls ledger and payments; expose POST /payments to the gateway"; the platform translates that into mesh resources.

~~~yaml
# values.yaml in a service repo: intent, not mesh internals
service:
  name: payments-api
  port: 8080
mesh:
  dependsOn: [ledger/ledger-api, fraud/fraud-scoring]   # generates Sidecar egress hosts or waypoint routes
  inbound:
    - from: edge/api-gateway
      methods: [POST, GET]
      paths: ["/payments", "/payments/*"]
    - from: orders/orders-api
      methods: [POST]
      paths: ["/payments"]
  timeouts: { default: 3s }
  canary: { enabled: true, analysis: standard-http }
# The platform chart renders AuthorizationPolicies, HTTPRoutes, Rollouts and alerts from this
~~~
pts: Golden-path templates express intent.
Surface response flags and authz explanations.
Realistic dev environments or cluster-connected local dev.
CI linting with clear messages.
Developers shouldn't need Envoy knowledge.

questions.q: A shared Kubernetes platform hosts workloads for several business units and external clients. How do you use the mesh for tenant isolation, and where is it insufficient?
questions.a:
### Mesh contributions
- **Identity per tenant workload** (service accounts per namespace per tenant).
- **Default-deny authorisation** at tenant namespace boundaries; cross-tenant calls only through explicit, reviewed policies or a shared API gateway.
- **Config isolation**: exportTo namespace-local; tenants cannot create VirtualServices for other tenants' hosts (admission policy).
- **Egress per tenant** via dedicated egress gateways (different source IPs for partner allow-lists).
- **Telemetry per tenant** for chargeback and SLOs.

### Insufficient alone
| Concern | Additional control |
|---|---|
| noisy neighbours (CPU, memory) | ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, node pools per tier |
| kernel-level isolation for untrusted code | sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata) or separate clusters |
| Kubernetes API access | RBAC per tenant namespace; no cluster-wide roles |
| shared node compromise | node pools per tenant class; ambient ztunnel is per node, so a node compromise affects all tenants on it |
| regulatory separation | separate clusters or meshes (federation) |

### Decision
Soft multi-tenancy (internal business units): shared mesh with strict namespaces. Hard multi-tenancy (external clients, regulated data): separate clusters or meshes.

  action: DENY
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        notNamespaces: ["tenant-acme-payments", "tenant-acme-ledger", "edge"]
---
# Admission rule (Kyverno, excerpt): VirtualService hosts must be within the tenant's namespaces
# deny if any(request.object.spec.hosts[] not ending with ".tenant-acme-*.svc.cluster.local" and not short name)
~~~
pts: Identity, default deny and config isolation per tenant.
Per-tenant egress and telemetry.
Resource quotas and node pools for noisy neighbours.
Sandboxing or separate clusters for untrusted or regulated tenants.
Soft vs hard multi-tenancy determines architecture.

questions.q: What is your three-year strategy for service-to-service networking given Gateway API (GAMMA), ambient and eBPF trends? How do you avoid lock-in while delivering value now?
questions.a:
### Trends
- **Gateway API for mesh (GAMMA)**: HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute attached to Services standardise mesh routing across implementations.
- **Sidecar-less data planes**: ambient (ztunnel plus waypoints), Cilium eBPF; per-pod proxies become the exception.
- **Workload identity standardisation**: SPIFFE across clusters, VMs and clouds.
- **Managed meshes** from cloud providers.

### Strategy
1. **Now**: deliver uniform mTLS and default-deny authorisation (audit value) using ambient where possible.
2. **Portable config**: new routing in Gateway API resources; keep vendor CRDs (VirtualService, EnvoyFilter) to a minimum and platform-owned.
3. **Identity first**: SPIFFE identities and enterprise PKI as the long-lived asset; the data plane is replaceable.
4. **Intent-based developer interface** (chart values) so the underlying mesh can change without touching teams.
5. **Measure and revisit** annually: overhead, incidents, evidence automation, cost.

### Avoiding lock-in
Lock-in is mostly in **policies and routing config** and in **team knowledge**; abstracting via Gateway API and golden-path templates keeps migration cost to a platform project rather than a 200-team project.

Write new routing in Gateway API.

cheat:
### What and why
Infrastructure layer for east-west traffic: mTLS and workload identity, service-level authorisation, traffic management, resilience, telemetry, without app changes. Costs: complexity, overhead, a new failure domain, platform team needed.

### Architecture
Data plane: Envoy sidecars, or ambient ztunnel per node (L4, HBONE on 15008) plus waypoints (L7). Control plane (istiod): xDS (listeners, routes, clusters, endpoints, secrets), CA, injection webhook. istiod down: traffic continues; no changes, scaling or cert rotation. Interception via iptables or CNI; native sidecars fix startup, shutdown and Job issues.

### Identity and mTLS
SPIFFE spiffe://trust-domain/ns/NS/sa/SA from service accounts (one per workload). Short-lived certs auto-rotated. PERMISSIVE for migration only; find plaintext via connection_security_policy telemetry; STRICT per namespace then mesh-wide; continuous negative tests. Enterprise PKI via plug-in intermediates or cert-manager istio-csr/Vault; dual-root bundles for rotation; expiry alerts.

### Authorisation
Order: CUSTOM, DENY, ALLOW (empty spec denies all). Principals, namespaces, methods, paths, JWT claims. RequestAuthentication only validates present tokens: require requestPrincipals. Service-level only: BOLA stays in apps. Default deny with allow-lists from a full business cycle of telemetry, dry-run first. Target team owns inbound policy. Layer with NetworkPolicy.

### Traffic and resilience
DestinationRule subsets, VirtualService or HTTPRoute weights and header matches; propagate cohort headers. Timeouts, bounded retries on safe conditions, outlier detection, connection pools as bulkheads (Little's law). One retry owner per hop. L7 per-request LB fixes HTTP/2 and gRPC pinning (ambient needs waypoint). Fault injection on synthetic traffic. Mirror only reads.

### Operations
Response flags: UF, UH, NR, UO, URX, UT, RBAC 403. istioctl analyze, proxy-status, proxy-config, describe, authz check. Revision-based canary upgrades with tags. exportTo namespace-local, Sidecar scoping. Kyverno guardrails: no PERMISSIVE, capped retries, no host hijack. Telemetry: trace headers must be propagated by apps; tune labels and logs. Egress: REGISTRY_ONLY, ServiceEntry, egress gateways plus firewalls.

### Multi-cluster
Single mesh (shared root, multi-primary or primary-remote, east-west gateways) vs federation (separate trust domains, narrow exports). Locality LB needs outlier detection; pin regional data owners; residency-aware failover.

### Limits
Not protected: compromised allowed workloads, app vulnerabilities, business abuse, supply chain, data at rest, insiders, Kafka topic authz. Kafka: L4 only, use native TLS and ACLs.

### Principal moves
Rollout in waves with sponsor, platform doing the work, scorecard and expiring exemptions. Don't adopt for small estates or without owners; alternatives: app TLS, OAuth, NetworkPolicy, resilience libraries, OTel. ADR: ambient with selective waypoints often wins. Operating model with platform SLOs. Cost: ambient and telemetry tuning. Sidecar-to-ambient: retarget L7 policies to waypoints. Gateway API (GAMMA) and intent-based templates to avoid lock-in.
